You use the subjunctive after cuando, en cuanto, hasta que, antes de que, después de que (for the future) and after para que (purpose).
When you get to Tokyo, call us.
As soon as I have news, I’ll write to you.
I’m not leaving until you promise me you’ll come.
I want to see you before you leave.
I’m leaving you my book so you don’t forget me.
To use cuando + SUBJUNCTIVE for the future (cuando llegues) and + indicative for habits (cuando llego).
To use en cuanto, hasta que, después de que the same way as cuando.
To know that antes de que ALWAYS takes the subjunctive.
To use para que + subjunctive (purpose for someone else) versus para + infinitive.
To say goodbye and make promises for the future.
Friday, at the club. Yuki has defended her PhD thesis. Everyone wants to celebrate, but Yuki has some news.
Congratulations, Dr Yuki! How did the defence go?
Very well, thank you. But I have to tell you something. I’ve been offered a job at the University of Tokyo.
That’s great! And when do you start?
In September. I’m leaving in a month.
A month? That’s very soon… And what will happen to the club when you leave?
That’s what I wanted to ask you. I want the club to carry on. Ana, could you run it when I’m not here?
Of course. But only if you promise me one thing: as soon as you get to Tokyo, you video call us.
Promise. And when I have my new flat, I’ll show you every corner.
Before you leave, we have to throw a farewell party. A proper one.
At my restaurant. And I’m not going back into the kitchen until everyone has sung karaoke. Even me.
You, Kenji? Singing? I have to see that before I leave!
And Tama? Does Mrs Suzuki know?
Not yet. I’ll tell her tomorrow, after she finishes her shift at the library. I’m so sorry.
Yuki, you taught us Japanese. Without you, Ana and I would never have met.
Don’t say that, or I’ll start crying…
Then cry. And while you’re here, we’ll make the most of every day. So you don’t miss us… or so you miss us a lot.
“nos eches de menos” = you miss us (subj.)
en-KWAN-to: run together, no pause after “en”. Don’t confuse it with “en cuanto a” (as for, regarding).
des-pe-DEE-da: the final d is very soft and almost disappears in fast speech in Spain: “despedía”.
e-CHAR-de-ME-nos. Echo de menos = I miss (in Spain). In Latin America people say “te extraño”.
After “cuando” you can have the indicative OR the subjunctive, depending on the time:
Cuando llego a casa, me ducho.
Cuando llegué a casa, me duché.
Cuando llegue a casa, me ducharé.
The classic mistake: “Cuando llegarás…” (future after cuando). It doesn’t exist in Spanish! NEVER put the future after cuando. For the future, use the subjunctive: Cuando llegues.

English has a similar rule: you say “when you ARRIVE”, never “when you will arrive”. In Spanish, the slot that English fills with the present takes the subjunctive: “when it will happen = subjunctive”.
2. En cuanto, hasta que, después de que, mientras
These time conjunctions follow EXACTLY the same rule as “cuando”: subjunctive for the future, indicative for habits and the past.
A simple exception to remember: “antes de que” ALWAYS takes the subjunctive, even in the past. Logical: what happens “before” hasn’t happened yet.
I left before it started raining. (imperfect subj., later in B1)
Same person → infinitive: Quiero verte antes de irme (I see, I leave). Different people → antes de que + subjunctive: antes de que te vayas (I see, you leave).
4. Para que: purpose for someone else
Estudio para aprobar. (I study, I pass)
Te explico para que apruebes. (I explain, you pass)
Ahorro para que mis hijos estudien.
“Para que” ALWAYS takes the subjunctive, like “antes de que”. The same goes for “sin que” (without): Se fue sin que nadie lo viera (He left without anyone seeing him).
English helps you: “so that” = para que + subjunctive. “I’m giving you the book so that you remember me” = Te doy el libro para que te acuerdes de mí.
In four chapters you’ve learned almost all the situations where the present subjunctive is used. The classic mnemonic is “WEIRDO + time”:
me alegra que, me da miedo que
es importante que, es normal que
te pido que, te aconsejo que
no creo que, dudo que, puede que
cuando llegues, antes de que, para que
In the next B1 unit you’ll learn the PAST subjunctive (si tuviera, quería que vinieras), which you’ve already seen a few times in the stories.
“When I have time, I’ll call you.”

I’m leaving you the book so you don’t forget me.
While you’re here, we’ll make the most of every day.

Yuki writes a list of everything she wants to do in Madrid before she leaves, and what she asks of her friends.
Things I want to do before I leave Madrid:
One: see the sunset from the Temple of Debod once more, before they close the park for works.
Two: eat churros with chocolate at San Ginés at six in the morning, while the city is still asleep.
Three: teach Mrs Suzuki to make video calls, so we can talk when I’m in Tokyo.
Four: leave Ana all my club notes, so she doesn’t have to start from scratch.
Five: ask Kenji for his ramen recipe. I know he won’t give it to me, but I’ll keep trying until he says yes.
Six: not cry at the airport. (I know it’s impossible, but I’m writing it down anyway.)
And I ask my friends just one thing: when you have holidays, come to Tokyo. I’ll be waiting for you with tea and a metro map.
¿Para qué quiere enseñar a la señora Suzuki a hacer videollamadas?
Para que puedan hablar cuando esté en Tokio
¿Qué le va a dejar a Ana?
The farewell party was on a Friday at the end of August. It was so hot that Kenji opened all the restaurant windows and hung lanterns at the door.
Everyone came: the club members, Yuki’s neighbours, her university colleagues and even the professor who had supervised her thesis, a very serious man who, according to Yuki, had never laughed.
Ana had prepared a surprise. When Yuki came in, everyone held up a sheet of paper. On each sheet was a Japanese word that Yuki had taught them over four years.
“Arigatō”. “Tomodachi”. “Ganbatte”. “Mata ne”. And on Mrs Suzuki’s sheet, written in shaky letters: “Okaeri”, which means “welcome home”.
Yuki covered her mouth with her hands. “That’s not fair,” she said. “I promised I wouldn’t cry until I got to the airport.”
“Promises about airports don’t count,” Mihai answered.
Kenji served dinner: one dish from each country in the club. There were gyoza, paella, pasta, sarmale and a huge potato tortilla made by Carmen.

As they ate, everyone shared a memory of Yuki. Carlos remembered the club’s first day, when there were only five people and Tama. Hanako said Yuki had helped her find a flat in her first week in Madrid.
Sofía said that, thanks to Yuki, she had learned not to put cheese in ramen. Kenji said that was the most important thing that had ever happened at the club. Everyone laughed.
Then came the karaoke. Kenji had promised he wouldn’t go back into the kitchen until everyone had sung. And he kept his promise.
Ana sang, and she sang very well. Carlos sang, very badly but with great passion. The serious professor sang a song from the eighties, and Yuki discovered that he could laugh after all.
At the end, Kenji took the microphone. The whole restaurant went quiet. Nobody had ever heard him sing.
He chose a very old Japanese song, one his mother used to sing to him when he was a child in Hiroshima. His voice was deep and a little shaky.
Nobody understood the lyrics except Yuki and Hanako. But there was no need. When he finished, Mrs Suzuki was crying, and Tama, in her arms, was purring.
It was already midnight when Mrs Suzuki came up to Yuki with a little wooden box.
“This is for you. Don’t open it until you’re on the plane.”
“Something so you don’t forget where your second home is.”
Yuki hugged her for a long time. Neither of them said anything. There was no need.
Two weeks later, on the plane, Yuki opened the little box. Inside was an old photograph of Kyoto, the same one Mihai had found at the flea market.
On the back of the photo, Mrs Suzuki had written a new note, in Japanese, in her small, neat handwriting.
“Fifty years ago I made the journey the other way: from Kyoto to Madrid. I was scared. I didn’t know anyone. But I found a family.”
“Now you’re making the journey back. Don’t be afraid. When you miss Madrid, look at this photo and remember: families aren’t lost through distance. They just change address.”
Yuki looked out of the window. Below, the lights of Madrid were getting smaller and smaller.
She cried, of course. She had broken the airport promise two weeks earlier, so now it didn’t matter.
But as she cried, she smiled. Because she knew that as soon as she landed in Tokyo, she would have to switch on her phone. And that a message would be waiting for her there.

And so it was. Fourteen hours later, the message said: “Okaeri, Yuki. The club is expecting you on Friday on video call. Don’t be late. Signed: Ana, Mihai, Kenji, Sofía, Carlos, Hanako, Mrs Suzuki… and Tama.”

Yuki laughed out loud in the airport corridor. A Japanese lady looked at her curiously. Yuki showed her the phone and explained, in Japanese, that she had a very big family in Spain. The lady smiled and said: “How lucky you are.” And Yuki thought that yes, she really was very lucky.

Text to read: The first video call
On Friday evening, the club calls Yuki in Tokyo.
Yuki! Can you see us? Can you hear us? We’re all here!
I can see you! It’s four in the morning here, but I don’t care. I’m so glad you’re all together.
Good, but I miss speaking Spanish. When I have holidays in December, I’m coming to Madrid. I promise!
We’ll be waiting for you. And Mrs Suzuki says don’t come back without bringing real green tea.
Tell her yes. And tell Tama I miss her… and not to eat so much while I’m not there.
